newsitem.title: UK: POLL-EU EXPECTED TO BASE EURO ON ERM PARITIES.
newsitem.headline: POLL-EU EXPECTED TO BASE EURO ON ERM PARITIES.

text.p: Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) is expected to form the basis for striking the value of the single currency due to be launched in 1999, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.
In the survey, carried out between August 6 and 8, 21 out of 32 contributors said the European Union (EU) would decide the value of the euro on ERM parities.
Five experts said the single currency, due to be launched with European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on January 1, 1999 would be based on average trading rates over a set period of time.
Another alternative, fixing the euro at the trading rates of the participating currencies on a specified day, received four votes and two said they expected the decision to be deferred.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in mid-June he hoped finance ministers and central bankers would reach a decision on how final exchange rates would be fixed for the euro at a September meeting in Luxembourg.

ERM parities have the blessing of EU central bankers, especially the Bundesbank, and because they are already fixed the potential for disruption and turbulence in the currency markets will be limited, analysts said.
"Deciding to use the parities will give the markets a guideline sooner rather than later, this will quell a lot of uncertainty," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
"An early decision is also a message from central banks -- if you speculate against us, you will get a bloody nose."
Eleven out of the 21 who predicted the use of ERM parities to set the value of the euro cited the Irish punt as a potential problem.

In recent months, the Irish currency has followed sterling's rise against other European currencies, causing severe strains within the ERM and fuelling speculation of a punt revaluation, analysts said.

Over the past week the punt has drifted back with sterling against the mark, but EMU experts say Ireland's strong trading links with Britain and the correlation between movements in the two currencies may come back to haunt EMU and euro stability.
Britain is not a member of the ERM.
Some economists believe a 10 percent revaluation, reversing a 10 percent devaluation in 1993, from the current central rate of 2.41 marks to 2.65 is inevitable.
But they said revaluation could be a recipe for trouble.

"A revaluation of the punt would open Pandora's box. Other countries who want a competitive advantage may decide they want to devalue their currencies," Grebe said. "And nobody knows where the fair value of the punt is."
Most of those who predicted the euro to be based on the trading levels on a specific day said it was the only method consistent with the Maastricht Treaty.

"They will stick to the treaty. There will be no legal issues or controversy if they adopt the strictest interpretation of the wording," said Raents Abma, economist at VNO-VCW employers' confederation in the Netherlands.
A reason given by respondents opting for an average rate over a period of time was that individual countries would find it difficult to manipulate the final rates.
Heidi Sherman, senior economist at the IFO institute in Germany, said use of an average rate was realistic, independent of ERM parities and free from an "accidental" rate being set on a specific day.
